frames.narration: The shop publishes one anycast address from 250 points of presence. Routing sends each client to the closest one, so the visitor lands in Frankfurt and the bot in Sao Paulo. An attack is split along the same lines: no single site sees all of it.

Before any HTTP, the point of presence deals with the packets. Spoofed SYNs are answered with SYN cookies, so half-open connections cost no memory, UDP to ports the shop does not use is dropped, and a per-source connection limit applies. Only real handshakes become requests.

states.pop: SYN cookies on, UDP junk dropped

frames.narration: The request is scored. The visitor has a normal browser fingerprint, a bot score of 8 out of 100 and a WAF score of 0, so it passes. The bot's headers and TLS fingerprint match a known scripting library: bot score 94. The WAF scores its query 2 points, below the blocking line of 5, because the request alone looks harmless.

The visitor's product page is in the cache of this point of presence, so it is returned from memory in a few milliseconds and the origin never hears about it. This is how most real traffic is absorbed.

The bot adds a random query string to every request, so a cache keyed by the full URL would always miss. The cache normalizes the key by ignoring parameters the page does not use. Because of the high bot score, the bot is first sent a challenge, which it cannot solve, and its request goes no further.

Meanwhile every point of presence reports its request rate. Normal is 4,000 requests per second, and the flood is 120,000, thirty times more. The detector waits for 2 seconds in a row above the learned limit, and for the origin to show strain, before it acts, so a flash sale is not mistaken for an attack.

Eight seconds of overload confirm it, and 4 more seconds push a rule to every point of presence: challenge every client that has no good reputation. The flood falls to about 6% of its size within 12 seconds. The challenge costs about 3% of real visitors who fail or leave, which is why it is switched on only for the attack.

states.filters: challenge on, about 3% of real visitors lost

frames.narration: A request that has to reach the origin, such as a checkout, goes through a private tunnel that the origin itself opens to the edge. The origin has no public address that accepts traffic from anywhere else.

An attacker who found the old origin address in a DNS history tries to bypass the shield. The packets are dropped at the origin's network boundary, because only the tunnel is allowed in, and none of the 120,000 requests per second ever arrives.

messages.label: direct to old origin IP: dropped
